title: Randomized versus quantum query complexity
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: An exposition of OpenAI's proof (2026) that the exponent 4 in the inequality R(f) <= C (1 + Q(f))^4 between the randomized and the quantum query complexity of total Boolean functions cannot be lowered: there are total functions F_(k,m) with Q about sqrt(m) and R about m^(2-1/k). The quantum upper bound and the quartic inequality are proved in full; the randomized lower bound uses one named hypothesis, the lower bound of Bansal and Sinha for the Forrelation function. The first lesson defines decision trees, the Forrelation function, and the functions F_(k,m) with their addressed cells and outward pointers. The second lesson defines the quantum query model and proves that measurements during a computation can be deferred without more queries. The third lesson proves amplitude amplification in a form that keeps the successful state fixed, and gives the quantum algorithm for the Forrelation function. The fourth lesson proves the tournament for probabilistic comparisons and the bound Q(F_(k,m)) <= C_k sqrt(m) (log m)^4. The fifth lesson proves the randomized lower bound by a coupling of a dummy input and a planted input and a lemma on guessing the answers of several independent inputs. The sixth lesson proves D(f) <= 1.5 * 10^6 Q(f)^4 for all total functions: the adversary bound, Huang's theorem on the sensitivity graph, and a deterministic algorithm.
prerequisites: core course Linear Algebra (B40): complex inner product spaces, unitary maps, eigenvalues of real symmetric matrices
finite probability: conditional probabilities, means, the inequalities of Markov and Chebyshev
the minimax theorem for finite games, proved in the course Large independent sets in three-colorable graphs (lesson Alignment of lists: patterns, minimax and Ramsey's theorem)
the lessons prove every other fact they use, except the named hypothesis (BS) of the first lesson, which is used only for the randomized lower bound

open_obligations: Named hypothesis (BS): the lower bound of Bansal and Sinha for the randomized query complexity of the k-fold Forrelation function with delta = 2^(-5k) (arXiv:2008.07003, Corollary 1.4). It is not proved in the programme; its proof uses Gaussian interpolation and bounds for Fourier coefficients of decision trees. Part 2 of Theorem 2.2, Corollary 2.3 and the statement that the exponent 4 is optimal depend on it. The quantum bound for F_(k,m) and the quartic inequality do not.

The bound for the size of the exact circuit (first lesson, Lemma 4.1) uses that integers of B bits are added, negated under a control bit and compared by circuits of a constant times B gates with two inputs; the lesson says how (bit by bit with a carry) and does not list the gates.

Attributions without a checked reference: the quartic inequality to Aaronson, Ben-David, Kothari, Rao and Tal, the adversary bound to Barnum, Saks and Szegedy, the signed matrix to Huang, the bound D <= bs deg to Midrijanis, the argument for several answers to Shaltiel and Drucker, on the authority of the manuscript; these papers were not read for the course. That an inequality with the exponent 3 had been conjectured is stated in the manuscript and in Bansal and Sinha (page 4).
The lessons were written and checked by one model in one session; they have not been checked by a second reader.
